marked/log.text:
The cardinality of a finite set $A$ is the number of elements in $A.$ 

Notice that the elements of our set 

$$
3, \quad 21, \quad 147, \quad 1\,029,\quad \ldots
$$

form a geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=7{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =7 \\  & =\frac{21}{3} \\  & =\frac{147}{21} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our geometric sequence, denoted $a_n,$ is given by

$$
a_n = a_1 r^{n-1} = 3(7^{n-1}) = \dfrac37(7)^n.
$$

Therefore, we can express $A$ in set-builder notation as follows:

$$
A = \left\{\dfrac37(7)^n : n\in \mathbb N,\: 1\leq n \leq N \right\}
$$

where $N\in \mathbb N$ is to be determined.

To find $N,$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{7}(7)^{N} & =5\,931\,980\,229 \\ {7}^{N} & =13\,841\,287\,201 \\ N & ={log}_{7}⁡(13\,841\,287\,201) \\ N & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(13\,841\,287\,201)}{{log}_{10}⁡(7)} \\ N & =12\end{aligned}
$$

bare/det.text:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 4 & 7\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 7\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-4)-2(7-3)+3(4-0) \\  & =-4-2\cdot 4+3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4-8+12 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 6-2\cdot 5 \\  & =18-10 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{2} & -2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{3}-(-2)\cdot 0 \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we expand the parentheses and simplify the resulting expression:

$$
3\cos^2 x \left(\sec^2 x -1\right) = 3\cos^2 x \sec^2 x - 3\cos^2 x
$$

Then, we use the identity $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ to further simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{cos}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-3{cos}^{2}⁡x & =3{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\right)}^{2}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{3{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{3\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}}{\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the identity $\sin^2 x = 1-\cos^2 x$ to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, as follows:

$$
3(1-\cos^2 x) = 3\cdot \sin^2 x = 3\sin^2 x
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
3\cos^2 x \left(\sec^2 x -1\right)= 3\sin^2 x.

Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](images/d0/d096d76118bc06b2d5c79d5017c0178d96fc84bff6f97d563b7b872d26e75d20.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\frac{3\pi }{2}<arg⁡(z)<2\pi .$

$$
\alpha =arctan⁡\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)≈0.620\,25.
$$

$$
\theta =arg⁡(z)=2\pi -0.620\,25≈5.66
$$

to two decimal places.

$$

$$

it is known that $\lim_{x\to 1}f(x)=3.$ What is the value of the constant $p?$

$p=$
{{field-1}}

In order for $\lim_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to be equal to $3,$ the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal to $3.$

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=3{e}^{\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}3{e}^{\,\,sin(x-1)} \\  & =3{e}^{\,\,sin(1-1)} \\  & =3{e}^{\,\,sin(0)} \\  & =3{e}^{0} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=p{x}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}(p{x}^{3}) \\  & =p\cdot {1}^{3} \\  & =p\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
